title: Steinway and Baldwin pianos
summary: Wilson prefers a nine-foot German Steinway for its response and reward for effort over louder-sounding pianos.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Not an American Steinway, but a German Steinway.
: Uh huh. That's your favorite piano, Steinway, right?

I have played a few of them, and I would have to get used to it; it doesn't speak out loud and clear like -- it's a more mellow and sweet toned piano, and it seems to me if you pressure it too much, it pressures you back, it hits you back -- you have to learn how to play it. The Steinway, you can be nervous and hit it too hard, it'll do whatever you put on it -- it'll just do, you know?

And some Baldwins, they're loud, and they're not loud enough, and you know they're too loud, and yet you feel like hitting them harder and harder and it's loud, but see, it don't feel loud. But it sounds loud. Yet, a Steinway feels loud when you hit it, and it is loud, too.
You get the reward, you know, if you work on it.
You get plenty of the satisfying sound for the amount of work you give it.
